# The Blue Hour

There's a time of day that doesn't quite belong to anyone.

You know the one. It comes after the sun has finished its business and gone, but before night has fully committed. The sky turns the color of a bruise that's almost healed — that uncertain purple-blue, the color of forgetting. The French call it *l'heure bleue*. The blue hour. They gave it a name because it demands one.

I want to talk about in-between things tonight.

I was seven when I learned that the future was real. Not in the way adults meant it — "save your money" and "study hard" and all that framing — but in the way that hit me in the chest at two in the morning while staring at the ceiling. The future was a real place. Somewhere out there, time was already happening without me. There was a Thursday in 2019 where I'd sit in a coffee shop in Portland and feel briefly, perfectly content. I didn't know it yet, but it was already weaving itself together. Every moment of my life was quietly assembling in the dark.

That thought should be terrifying. Sometimes it is.

But mostly it feels like a door left open in a house I haven't explored yet.

---

My grandmother kept mothballs in cedar closets and told stories like she was breathing — automatically, unconsciously, the way you do the thing that keeps you alive. She never understood why anyone would want to write fiction. "The world is already strange enough," she'd say, smoothing her apron. "Why would you add to the strangeness?"

She had a point. I've been writing for twenty years and I still can't beat reality for sheer, bewildering weirdness. I can't imagine anything stranger than this: that there are nearly eight billion people walking around on this rock right now, each one of them with a whole universe behind their eyes, and most of them are thinking about lunch or parking spots or what someone said to them three days ago that they should have responded to differently. And I'm one of them. And you're one of them. And neither of us is more real than the other.

That's the strangest thing I know.

---

I've been thinking about rivers.

Not metaphorical ones. Actual rivers. The way they don't care about straight lines. The way a river just *goes* — around obstacles, over rocks, through valleys, carving canyons over centuries with nothing but patience and persistence and a kind of stubborn flow that would make a philosopher weep. A river has never once worried about productivity. A river has never asked itself if it's fulfilling its potential. It just moves.

There's a lesson there that I've failed to learn approximately four thousand times.

---

Somewhere right now, a child is falling asleep while their parent hums a song that they themselves were sung to sleep with, passed down like a gene, a melody that crosses generations without anyone writing it down. Somewhere right now, two strangers are standing in an elevator not speaking. Somewhere right now, someone is holding a letter they haven't opened because opening it makes it real.

The world is made of these moments. The unsung lullabies. The silent elevator rides. The unopened letters.

We talk about the big things — wars and elections and discoveries and catastrophes — and sure, those matter. But I think the real texture of being alive is in the small, quiet things. The way someone pauses before laughing, just barely, as if deciding whether the world deserves their joy in this moment. (It does. It always does.)

---

I don't know what this is. It's not an essay. It's not a poem. It's not a story. It's just words in a room, like people in a room, arranged in some way that feels like coherence even if it isn't. Stream of consciousness. River of thought. Whatever you want to call it.

Maybe it's just proof that I was here.

Maybe that's all any of this is. Proof of being here. Proof that between one breath and the next, something existed — a thought, a feeling, a Tuesday afternoon where the light hit the kitchen table at just the right angle and made the whole world look like a painting by someone who understood that beauty is mostly about timing.

---

Here's what I know:

The blue hour passes. Night comes. Morning comes after. Everything that's in-between resolves itself into something else if you just let it move. The river keeps going. The songs get hummed. The letters get opened or they don't.

And sometimes, just sometimes, a stranger on the internet writes 900 words of nothing and someone reads it and feels less alone.

That's enough.

That's more than enough.
